panels.figure_caption: DISH criteria clarifications. a Shows 3 levels of DISH discontinuous flowing ossifications (white arrows); 3 contiguous interdisc levels are needed. The non-flowing or partial ossifications are marked with arrowheads. b1, b2 By changing the W/L a spine can simulate DISH or flowing osteophyte (arrows). c Difference between degenerative osteophytes and DISH; less than 90° and sharp corners indicate degenerative disease. The vertebrae level below shows a flowing osteophyte with less than 90° corner but no sharp corners. d The pattern of flowing ossifications is typical of DISH and not characteristic of osteoarthritic degenerative disease. There is no facet ankylosis and mild discopathy; flowing ossifications are leading

On the basis of the ensuing discussion, a set of reference images was defined and the DISH criteria were refined with four clarifications (Fig. 1):Fig. 1DISH criteria clarifications. a Shows 3 levels of DISH discontinuous flowing ossifications (white arrows); 3 contiguous interdisc levels are needed. The non-flowing or partial ossifications are marked with arrowheads. b1, b2 By changing the W/L a spine can simulate DISH or flowing osteophyte (arrows). c Difference between degenerative osteophytes and DISH; less than 90° and sharp corners
DISH is established when (at least) four contiguous vertebrae or, alternatively, three contiguous disc levels are bridged (Fig. 1a).

Window width and level require fixed (Bone) settings (Fig. 1b1, b2) to prevent false positive and false negative cases, which may result from changing the density of longitudinal ligaments. It was also decided to use a single viewing plane to limit observer variation and we uniformly chose the sagittal plane to optimally assess DISH.

in_text_mentions: ra-articular bridging osteophytes located ventrally to the SIJs, similar to flowing osteophytes in the spine, are commonly seen in DISH patients, resulting from enthesopathy of the involved ligament (Figure 7A) [67,68]. in_text_mentions: Another phenomenon known to coexist with DISH is an elongation of the styloid process, which results from entheseal calcification and ossification of the stylohyoid ligament (Figure 4A) [38,39,40,41]. In rare cases, this elongation has been reported to cause craniofacial or cervical pain, termed Eagle syndrome [42]. In a study comparing the length of the styloid process, as measured by CT, between subjects with DISH (as per Resnick and Niwayama criteria), subjects with AS (as per modified New York criteria), and healthy controls, the average lengths of the styloid process in DISH and AS were s

s of varying degrees [44]. OPLL is a distinct entity that may appear without accompanying pathologies, with an incidence of up to 4% [45,46]. It has been reported to be associated with DISH, AS, and diabetes mellitus [45,46], with a concomitance rate of 57.14% for cervical OPLL accompanying DISH (Figure 4B) [47]. Both DISH and OPLL are primarily observed in elderly males and have a reported association with low glucose tolerance and obesity [47]. A shared local inflammatory pathogenesis has been suggested as the basis of both entities; however, this hypothesis needs further corroboration [48].

The scan shows a flowing ossification of the anterolateral spine with bridging over more than four contiguous vertebral bodies

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Lateral plain radiograph of the cervical spine in a 69-year-old male with DISH, showing solid bridging new bone formation extending over at least four vertebral bodies - classic DISH morphology in the cervical spine. B: Sagittal CT of the thoracic spine in a 72-year-old male with DISH, showing flowing anterolateral ossification bridging more than four contiguous vertebral bodies with relatively intact intervertebral discs and apophyseal joints - classic 'flowing candle wax' appearance. C: Axial CT of the cervical spine corresponding to the radiograph in panel A (69-year-old male with DISH), showing symmetrical hyperostosis anterior to the vertebral body highlighted in yellow, with possible tracheal displacement - characteristic of cervical DISH morphology. D: Axial CT of the mid-thoracic spine in a 58-year-old male with DISH, showing right anterolateral new bone formation highlighted in yellow with the aorta on the left anterolateral...
panels.attribution_text: Bakker et al. Morphological characteristics of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis in the cervical spine.. PloS one 2017. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0188414. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Typical examples of newly formed bone due to DISH in the cervical and thoracic spine. (A) Plain lateral radiograph shows a 69 year old male with DISH in the cervical spine. A solid formation of new bone is extending over at least four vertebral bodies. (B) Computed tomography (CT) visualizes the thoracic spine of a 72 year old male in the sagittal view. The scan shows a flowing ossification of the anterolateral spine with bridging over more than four contiguous vertebral bodies. The intervertebral discs and apophyseal joints are relatively intact in both images. (C + D) The CT scans in axial view demonstrate the differences in position of the new bone formation depending on the region. (C) The CT scan of the cervical spine corresponds to the radiographic image (A) and demonstrates symmetrical hyperostosis (yellow) anterior to the vertebral body and possible displacement of the trachea. (D) The axial CT of the mid thoracic spine in a 58 year old male with DISH shows the newly formed bone on the right anterolateral side with the aorta clearly located on the left anterolateral side.
in_text_mentions: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) is a systemic condition characterized by ossification of the spine and peripheral entheses [1]. The typical changes related to DISH occur most frequently in the anterolateral part of the thoracic spine, contralateral to the descending thoracic aorta, with bridging ossifications that resemble flowing candle wax in the lateral view (Fig 1) [2,3].

ing, flowing pattern [8]. In the cervical spine, however, the vertebral arteries and common, internal and external carotid arteries are located symmetrically and laterally to the vertebral bodies and segmental arteries (at least those of any significant caliber) crossing the vertebral bodies horizontally are absent [9]. If the hypothesis that large vessels prevent the formation of new bone in DISH is true, the newly formed bone in the cervical spine can be expected to be located in the midline and grow in a ventral direction, eventually leading to displacement of esophagus and trachea (Fig 1).

Plain anteroposterior and lateral cervical spine radiographs confirmed the diagnosis of DISH and showed a prominent anterior osteophyte at the C4-C5 level, causing posterior pharyngeal indentation, as illustrated in Figure 1. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Sagittal CT of an 88-year-old male cadaveric spine showing flowing anterolateral ossification of the thoracic spine, a classic DISH finding. The caption explicitly attributes the newly formed bone to DISH. B: 3D reconstructed CT of the same cadaveric specimen showing the flowing anterolateral ossification characteristic of DISH. The caption confirms this is the same DISH case. C: Macroscopic photograph of the cadaveric DISH spine specimen showing the relationship between the newly formed bone (β) and the anterior longitudinal ligament (α) at T5-T8, directly illustrating the ALL bone bridging finding central to the article's DISH focus.

findings.label: Peripheral enthesophyte formation
findings.evidence: osteitis pubis with sclerosis and erosions of the pubic symphysis

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real patient AP pelvic radiograph from a DISH cohort article; caption and in-text explicitly report osteitis pubis at the pubic symphysis, an enthesopathy manifestation significantly more frequent in DISH patients (11.5% vs 4.2%). B: Real patient AP pelvic radiograph; caption and in-text document bilateral iliac crest, ischiopubic and greater trochanter enthesopathy, all significantly more prevalent in DISH patients (ischiopubic 28.5% vs 4.0%; iliac crest 56.2% vs 16.8%). C: Real patient lateral radiograph; caption and in-text describe flowing thoracolumbar bridging ossification, interspinous ligament ossification and aortic calcifications, hallmark and associated radiographic features of DISH (all significantly higher in DISH patients).

plate_findings.evidence: burst fracture of Th12 (asterisk)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Sagittal T2WI MRI of a 66-year-old patient with DISH (article title and in-text context) showing a burst fracture of Th12, spinal cord injury, and subdural hematoma. The fracture is a known DISH-related chalk-stick fracture manifestation. b: Sagittal T1WI MRI of the same DISH patient showing the Th12 burst fracture as low signal and the subdural hematoma as hyperintense. Supports DISH-related spinal fracture. c: Transverse T2WI MRI at the level of the Th12 fracture in a DISH patient, showing a subdural hematoma contained within the dural sac and pressed against the spinal cord. Fracture context from the overall figure and article. d: Transverse T1WI MRI at the same level, showing the subdural hematoma with higher intensity than the spinal cord in a DISH patient with a Th12 burst fracture.
panels.attribution_text: Vierunen et al. Post-traumatic spinal hematoma in diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH).. European radiology 2023. doi:10.1007/s00330-023-09866-9. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: A 66-year-old patient fell three meters off a ladder on his stomach and was unable to move his lower limbs. A sagittal T2WI from an MRI scan revealed a spinal cord injury (arrow) caused by a burst fracture of Th12 (asterisk). Anteriorly to the spinal cord is a hyperintense spinal hematoma (arrowhead) visible in the subdural space (a). On sagittal T1WI, the subdural hematoma (arrowhead) appears hyperintense compared to the spinal cord (arrow). The burst fracture is shown as a low-intensity area on T1WI representing multiple fracture lines and oedema across the vertebral body (asterisk) (b). On transverse T2WI, the subdural hematoma (arrowhead) is contained within the dural sac and pressed against the spinal cord (arrow) (c). On transverse T1WI, the subdural hematoma (arrowhead) shows a higher intensity compared to the posteriorly located spinal cord (arrow) (d). MRI = magnetic resonance imaging, Th12 = twelfth thoracic vertebra

plate_findings.evidence: DISH signs in TL spine
only one enthesophyte (K)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (AP, MP, PP). AP: Radiographs of a 54-year-old male showing DISH signs in the thoracolumbar spine with a single peripheral enthesophyte at the knee and no hip involvement, consistent with the axial pattern described in the caption. [raw subtype: axial pattern] MP: Radiographs of a 70-year-old male showing an ankylosed spinal column with severe coxopathy and more than three peripheral enthesophytes, consistent with the mixed pattern described in the caption. [raw subtype: mixed pattern] PP: Radiographs of a 68-year-old female showing no spinal involvement but almost all peripheral entheses affected, with suspicion of cervical spine involvement. This represents the peripheral pattern that does not fulfill Resnick criteria but is proposed as a DISH phenotype in the article. [raw subtype: peripheral pattern]
panels.attribution_text: Clavaguera et al. Identifying Clinicoradiological Phenotypes in Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis: A Cross-Sectional Study.. Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania) 2021. doi:10.3390/medicina57101005. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: DISH patterns. Legend: AP: male 54 years, 10 years evolution. DISH signs in TL spine and only one enthesophyte (K) with no hip involvement. MP: male 70 years, 20 years evolution. Ankylosed column. Severe coxopathy. More than three peripheral enthesophytes (E, K, A). PP: female 68 years, 18 years evolution. No spine involvement, suspicion in CC. Almost all entheses affected (E, MT, K, A, C). DISH: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis; AP: axial pattern; MP: mixed pattern; PP: peripheral pattern; TL: thoracolumbar; E: elbows; MT: major trochanter; K: knees; A: Achilles; C: calcaneus; CC: cervical spine.
in_text_mentions: Based on previous observations, we proposed three clinical-radiological patterns: (a) peripheral pattern (PP) for patients who did not fulfil the Resnick criteria but who presented ≥3 peripheral enthesopathies (probable or possible Utsinger categories) with or without vertebral spine manifestations; (b) axial pattern (AP) for patients who met the Resnick criteria but who presented <3 peripheral enthesopathies; and (c) mixed pattern (MP) for patients who met the Resnick criteria but who presented ≥3 peripheral enthesopathies (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single-panel sagittal cervical CT of a real patient with an arrow indicating esophageal impression. The caption explicitly attributes the findings to advanced diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis and names specific captioned manifestations: prominent anterior marginal osteophytes at C5-C6 and significant impression on the esophageal lumen. Flowing anterolateral vertebral ossification, the hallmark of DISH, is also visibly present along the cervical spine. Disease attribution is unambiguous from both caption and article title.
panels.attribution_text: Lopez Menchero Mora et al. Clinical Image: Esophageal Compression Secondary to Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.113221. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Computed Tomography (CT) Sagittal and axial cervical CT images showing prominent anterior marginal osteophytes, particularly at C5-C6, causing significant impression on the esophageal lumen (arrow). Findings are compatible with advanced diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.
in_text_mentions: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrated marked posterior pharyngoesophageal compression (Figure 2). CT revealed prominent anterior marginal osteophytes, particularly at C5-C6, causing significant indentation of the esophageal lumen. These imaging findings were consistent with DISH (Figure 3). MRI demonstrated ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament with bridging ossification across C3-C4 and C4-C5. Prominent right anterolateral anterior osteophytes were also identified at C5-C6 and C7-T1, further supporting the diagnosis of DISH (Figure 4).

panels.rationale: Preoperative sagittal cervical spine CT from a real human patient (prior triage: keep, radiology, not third-party). The image visibly demonstrates flowing anterior ossification/autofusion of the cervical spine (C4-T1) and a lucency through a C6-7 syndesmophyte, which are direct manifestations of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis as stated in the caption and in-text; the article title and case context attribute these findings to early DISH. The focal ossified PLL (OPLL) is also explicitly captioned but is not in the allowed vocabulary, so it is recorded as a proposed finding rather than used for disease attribution. No diagnostic arrows/callouts are overlaid (only technical scan text and scale), and no skin, ethnicity, or further staging details are given.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Lateral standing whole-spine radiograph of a human patient from a DISH case report, visibly demonstrating flowing anterolateral ossification along the thoracic and lumbar vertebral bodies (Th2-L5), the hallmark radiographic manifestation of DISH; the article title and in-text confirm DISH attribution and exclude sacroiliitis/HLA-B27 disease. B: Sagittal CT multiplanar reconstruction of the whole spine from the same human DISH case, showing the flowing anterolateral vertebral ossification and the clearly opened L2-L3 intervertebral space corresponding to the symptomatic pseudoarthrosis; CT in DISH context directly supports disease attribution, so it qualifies as a target-disease image.

panels.rationale: Single sagittal MRI (photographed from film) of a human patient's cervical spine. The caption and in-text explicitly attribute the elongated ossification of the anterior vertebral bodies, with spiky anterior spurs at C5-C6, to DISH in a case report titled "Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis as a cause of progressive dysphagia." The visible flowing anterior vertebral ossification and anterior cervical osteophytes are classic DISH findings and match two vocabulary keys. Image quality is modest (dark photograph of a film view-box) but the cervical spine, vertebral bodies, and anterior ossification remain interpretable; prior caption triage also routed this figure to keep with no third-party concern. Esophageal compression is not directly visible on this MRI, so that finding is omitted. No age, ethnicity, or skin is shown; the "A" markers are MRI orientation labels, not annotations.

Although the caption labels it 'MRI,' the markedly bright cortical bone with sharp osseous detail and the 10 cm scale are characteristic of a CT bone-window sagittal reconstruction rather than MRI (where cortical bone is dark); the matching vocabulary finding for anterior cervical osteophytes is likewise categorized under CT. The image shows prominent anterior osteophytes of the cervical vertebral bodies exerting mass effect on the adjacent airway, matching the in-text report of anterior osteophytes at C2-3 and C6-7/T1 with anterior displacement of the laryngopharynx and trachea. Together with the article title (DISH of the cervical spine as an unusual cause of difficult intubation), this is a real human-patient image of a DISH manifestation. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or provided in-text; no skin is shown. There are no diagnostic annotation markers (arrows/arrowheads), only scanner scale text. Attribution to DISH is strong; confidence is slightly reduced because the caption modality (MRI) conflicts with the CT appearance.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Gross specimen photograph of the anterior view of human upper cervical vertebrae (C1-C3) from the DISH case report, showing an osteophyte of the anterior longitudinal ligament (green arrow) and an osteophyte of the alar ligament (red arrow) — specific ligamentous ossification manifestations of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis. B: Gross specimen photograph of the posterior view of human upper cervical vertebrae (C1-C3) from the same DISH case report; the in-text mention notes similar changes with clearer visualization of C1 osteophytes, which is a specific ossification manifestation of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis. panels.figure_caption: Histological appearance of a representative motion segment with horizontal presentation of ectopic mineralization associated with DISH. Images correspond to the specimen shown in Fig. 1b, T6-7. a Digital radiograph of the intact tissue prior to decalcification showing the localization of ectopic mineral within the motion segment (contoured by dotted yellow line). VB vertebral bone, IVD intervertebral disc. b Representative section stained with hematoxylin and eosin demonstrating the appearance of the intact section; scale bar represents 10 mm. The yellow box corresponds to an anterior region with features of heterotopic ossification imaged with a 10× objective (c–e), while the white box corresponds to a transition region from heterotopic ossification to the underlying fibrocartilage annulus fibrosus imaged with a 20× objective (f–h). c, f stained with hematoxylin and eosin; d, g stained with Masson’s trichrome; e, h the hematoxylin and eosin stained sections shown in c and f visualized with polarized light. Scale bars for c–h represent 100 µm. c–e Highlight features of heterotopic ossification along the anterior aspect of the motion segment, including compartmentalized bone marrow cavity (black asterisk) and organized lamellar bone (black arrowheads). f–h Characteristics of primary woven bone (black arrows) and organized nests of chondrocytes (white asterisk) associated with endochondral ossification. in_text_mentions: Twelve regions of the spine containing ectopic mineral structures at individual motion segments were isolated (Supplementary Fig. S1) to assess the histological appearance of affected tissues. Figure 2 is representative of a motion segment with the morphological features of “horizontal” and “discontinuous-patchy” mineralization; Fig. 3 is representative of a motion segment with the morphological features of “horizontal” mineralization; and Fig. 4 is representative of a motion segment with the morphological features of “vertical” mineralization. As a reference, Supplementary Fig. S2 is represen

IVDs within the intact motion segments examined demonstrated consistent histological features (n = 12: Figs. 2–4). Although radiographic IVD height was maintained in keeping with Resnick’s criteria,2 the nucleus pulposus was granular in appearance, indicative of mild-to-moderate degeneration. In all sections examined, varying degrees of IVD degeneration were observed. The characteristics of degeneration included the loss of a distinct transition between the nucleus pulposus and surrounding annulus fibrosus (Figs. 2b and 4b) as well as moderate-to-severe disorganization of the lamellar structur

In all motion segments assessed, histological examination confirmed the radiographic selection criterion of a mineralized tissue bridge between the superior and inferior vertebrae across an IVD (Figs. 2–4). In general, cellular indications of inflammation were absent from areas of ectopic mineralization, although small areas of scattered inflammatory cells (primarily macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells) and neovascularization were noted. Tremendous heterogeneity was, however, noted in the histological features of the ectopic mineral structures associated with DISH.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Sagittal CT of a DISH patient showing flowing anterolateral vertebral ossification and a transverse fracture through the ankylosed T11-T12 spine (arrowhead), consistent with a chalk-stick fracture in DISH. Real human patient image of the configured disease. B: Sagittal T1-weighted MRI showing a low-intensity area in T11-T12 vertebrae (arrow), representing the vertebral compression fracture in a DISH patient described in the caption and in-text. Real human patient image of the configured disease. C: Sagittal T2-weighted MRI showing a high-intensity area in T11-T12 vertebrae (arrow), representing bone marrow edema from the vertebral compression fracture in a DISH patient. Real human patient image of the configured disease.

panels.figure_caption: Measurement of cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine skin thickness using sagittal whole-spine CT. The average skin thickness at the cervical (4-5, C5-6, C6-7 disc levels), thoracic (T7-8, T8-9, T9-10 disc levels), and lumbar (L2-3, L3-4, L4-5 disc levels) is defined as skin thickness.
in_text_mentions: Analysis was performed using a 64-slice detector CT scanner (Canon Aquilion; Canon Medical System Co., Tochigi, Japan) with 1.0 mm thick axial slices in the bone window setting (window: 2000; level: 200). Skin thickness was categorized into two groups based on the median value using a cutoff of 4 mm. The average skin thickness at the cervical (C4-5, C5-6, C6-7 disc levels), thoracic (T7-8, T8-9, T9-10 disc levels), and lumbar (L2-3, L3-4, L4-5 disc levels) regions was determined from sagittal cross-sectional images using whole spine CT (Figures 1, 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Sagittal CT of thoracolumbar spine in a DISH patient showing flowing anterolateral vertebral ossification with overlaid segmental disc angle measurement lines. Real patient radiology image with visible DISH manifestation. b: Sagittal CT of lumbar spine in a DISH patient showing flowing anterolateral vertebral ossification with overlaid lumbar lordosis measurement lines. Real patient radiology image with visible DISH manifestation. c: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of a DISH participant showing extensive flowing anterolateral ossification along the thoracolumbar spine. Real patient radiology image with clearly visible DISH manifestation. d: Axial CT image from a DISH patient showing a vertebral level with anterior bony ossification and measurement line through the center of the spinous process. Real patient image with visible but less prominent DISH manifestation; panel primarily illustrates measurement methodology.

panels.figure_caption: Illustration of the measurement of sagittal parameters in a DISH patient using a three-dimensional CT image. a: Segmental disc angle (SDA) was determined by measuring the angle between the superior and inferior endplates of each disc in the thoracolumbar and lumbar spine; b: Lumbar lordosis (LL) was measured between the superior endplate of L1 and the sacral plate; c: A three-dimensional CT reconstruction image of this DISH participant; d: Sagittal parameters were measured through the center of the spinous processes. Segmental lordosis is signified by positive values, whereas segmental kyphosis is characterized by negative values

The sagittal parameters on images from three-dimensional CT were evaluated by drawing tangential lines through the center of spinous processes (Fig. 2c and d). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Axial CT from a DISH cross-sectional study showing ankylosis with bony excrescence at the left costovertebral joint. The in-text explicitly links this costovertebral fusion/ossification of the radiate ligament to DISH (compared between DISH(+) and DISH(−) groups), and the article title is DISH-focused. The insertional/enthesopathic ossification at the costovertebral joint is a recognized but less common (variant) manifestation of DISH; the specific costovertebral terms are not in the vocabulary, so they are proposed. b: Axial CT showing bone bridging across the right costovertebral joint (arrow), the same hyperostotic costovertebral manifestation evaluated in the DISH cohort and compared between DISH(+) and DISH(−) groups per the in-text. Disease attribution to DISH is well supported; the manifestation is a variant (costovertebral rather than classic flowing anterolateral vertebral ossification), with costovertebral-specific terms proposed...

panels.figure_caption: Evaluation of hyperostosis around the costovertebral joint. The cross-sectional CT image passing through the costovertebral joint from T1 vertebra to the T12 vertebra was used to evaluate the hyperostosis around the costovertebral joint. (a) There is ankylosis and excrescence in the left costovertebral joint (white arrow). (b) There is bone bridging in the right costovertebral joint (black arrow).
in_text_mentions: the T1 vertebra to the T12 vertebra was used in this evaluation. In reference to the report by Sawagami et al. [9], the ankylosing or bone bridging of the costovertebral joint was recorded when the complete fusion and osseous outgrowth (ossification of the radiate ligament of the head of the rib) was apparent at the level of the costovertebral joint. Cases showing these findings in even one site within the area from the T1 vertebra to T12 vertebra were judged to show the costovertebral fusion, and the number of these cases was compared between the DISH (+) group and DISH (−) group (Figure 2).

The aorta‐osteophyte distance in flat osteophytes was significantly larger than that in concave osteophytes (5.2 ± 2.1 vs.3.2 ± 2.1mm, p<0.01), while there was no significant difference in osteophyte area between flat and concave osteophytes (252.8 ± 123.1 vs.284.6 ± 129.6mm2, p = 0.174). As shown in Figures 4 and 5, the aorta‐osteophyte distance of flat osteophytes is significantly larger than that of concave in most segments, including T7, T8, T9, T11, T12, L1, and L2. It means that the aorta was more closer to the concave than flat osteophytes (Figure 5).

om the left side to the middle of the vertebrae, the osteophytes gradually shifted from the right side alone of the vertebra (T5‐T10) to both right and left sides of the vertebra (T11‐L4), and the left margin of the osteophyte shows progression towards the left, while the right margin remains unchanged (Figure 3). In the 3‐D CT reconstruction of the spine in DISH patients (Figure 4), the aorta is clearly traced in the osteophytes in front of the spine. This vividly figured out that the relative spatial position of the aorta and osteophytes in DISH patients varied in different vertebral levels.

panels.attribution_text: Fournier et al. Dystrophic calcification and heterotopic ossification in fibrocartilaginous tissues of the spine in diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH).. Bone research 2020. doi:10.1038/s41413-020-0091-6. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Histological appearance of a representative motion segment with vertical presentation of ectopic mineralization associated with DISH. Images correspond to the specimen shown in Fig. 1a, T4–5. a Digital radiograph of the intact tissue prior to decalcification showing the localization of ectopic mineral within the motion segment (contoured by dotted yellow line). VB vertebral bone, IVD intervertebral disc. b Representative section stained with hematoxylin and eosin demonstrating the appearance of the intact section; scale bar represents 10 mm. The yellow box corresponds to the region within the fibrocartilage of the IVD with a discrete amorphous calcification imaged with a 20× objective (c–e). The white box corresponds to a region of heterotopic ossification along the anterior aspect of the IVD imaged with a 20× objective (f–h). The black box corresponds to the discrete calcification within the anterior longitudinal ligament imaged with 4× and 20× objectives (i–k). c, f, i Stained with hematoxylin and eosin; d, g, j stained with Masson’s trichrome; and e, h, k the hematoxylin and eosin stained sections visualized with polarized light. Scale bars for c–k represent 100 µm. c–e Highlight an amorphous region of dystrophic calcification localized within the annulus fibrosus (asterisk) and characterized by a granular appearance and variable eosinophilic staining. f–h A region of heterotopic ossification marked by organized osteons (black arrowheads). i–k Reveal an area of dystrophic calcification (black arrows) localized within the anterior longitudinal ligament (contoured by black dotted lines). k Corresponds to the dotted outline in j. All images are oriented as shown in a
in_text_mentions: morphological features of “horizontal” and “discontinuous-patchy” mineralization; Fig. 3 is representative of a motion segment with the morphological features of “horizontal” mineralization; and Fig. 4 is representative of a motion segment with the morphological features of “vertical” mineralization. As a reference, Supplementary Fig. S2 is representative of a motion segment with no evidence of ectopic mineralizations from a spine that did not meet the diagnostic criteria for DISH. In Figs. 2–4, digital radiographs are paired with low-magnification views of the intact motion segment to correla

IVDs within the intact motion segments examined demonstrated consistent histological features (n = 12: Figs. 2–4). Although radiographic IVD height was maintained in keeping with Resnick’s criteria,2 the nucleus pulposus was granular in appearance, indicative of mild-to-moderate degeneration. In all sections examined, varying degrees of IVD degeneration were observed. The characteristics of degeneration included the loss of a distinct transition between the nucleus pulposus and surrounding annulus fibrosus (Figs. 2b and 4b) as well as moderate-to-severe disorganization of the lamellar structur

In all motion segments assessed, histological examination confirmed the radiographic selection criterion of a mineralized tissue bridge between the superior and inferior vertebrae across an IVD (Figs. 2–4). In general, cellular indications of inflammation were absent from areas of ectopic mineralization, although small areas of scattered inflammatory cells (primarily macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells) and neovascularization were noted. Tremendous heterogeneity was, however, noted in the histological features of the ectopic mineral structures associated with DISH.

in_text_mentions: A 71-year-old man was hit by a car while crossing the road and was rushed to our hospital. A plain computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a vertebral fracture of the third lumbar vertebra associated with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (Figure 1A and 1B arrow). A subsequent contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a large hematoma in the abdominal cavity (Figure 2A arrow head), and the inferior vena cava was trapped at the fracture site (Figure 2B arrow) (1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Sagittal T2-weighted cervical spine MRI of a 73-year-old man explicitly captioned as DISH; the image demonstrates the hallmark flowing anterolateral vertebral ossification (candle-wax bridging) with partial C6-C7 ankylosis and disc height loss, plus enlarged anterior cervical osteophytes causing dysphagia. Clear disease attribution and textbook radiologic presentation. B: Companion sagittal T1-weighted cervical spine MRI from the same captioned figure of a 73-year-old man with DISH and dysphagia; shows the same flowing anterolateral ossification with anterior bridging osteophytes and partial C6-C7 ankylosis. Real patient image with unambiguous DISH attribution and classic radiologic appearance.

in_text_mentions: Following assessment in the clinic, standing thoracolumbar radiographs and CT scan were arranged (Figure 2). The standing thoracolumbar radiographs were felt to be sub-optimal, but within the limitations of the study, the T12 fracture appeared to have worsened from initial radiographs, and with multi-level degenerative disc disease in the form of prominent anterior osteophyte formation was noted. On the basis of this imaging, it was felt that instrumentation was the best option to achieve adequate analgesia through spinal stabilisation and fracture union.

in_text_mentions: Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a mixed ventilatory disorder, with a vital capacity (%VC) of 68.3% and a forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁%) of 40.3% (Table 1). In the thoracic and lumbar spine, fusion of adjacent vertebral bodies due to ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament was noted, consistent with DISH (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: CT revealed prominent anterior ossification at the cervicothoracic junction, accompanied by bony proliferation on the posterior surface of the sternum. These structural changes resulted in anteroposterior compression of the trachea (Figure 3). Based on these radiological findings, the patient was diagnosed with airway stenosis due to DISH and sternal bone overgrowth. Surgical resection of the bony structures was subsequently planned.

panels.rationale: Single-panel sagittal T2 MRI from a case report titled 'Posterior Percutaneous Screw Fixation to Treat Vertebral Fracture Non-union in Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis'. The image is a genuine untreated patient radiologic image (prior triage: keep, real patient, no third-party). The red arrow marks a T12 fracture non-union, corresponding to a chalk-stick-type fracture through the ankylosed DISH spine - a classic, characteristic DISH complication. Anterior vertebral ossification consistent with DISH is also visible along the contiguous vertebral levels. Caption additionally notes endplate changes (not in vocabulary). No skin shown, and no age or ethnicity stated in caption or in-text.

in_text_mentions: Plain radiographs were arranged by his GP three weeks following his fall and revealed a minor wedge fracture of the T12 body with uncertain chronicity. Repeat imaging three months later suggested worsening of the fracture. Upon receipt of referral to our services, six months following his original injury, and prior to clinic attendance, he underwent an MRI scan on which there was evidence of fracture non-union (Figure 1).

A: Sagittal CT shows the hallmark flowing anterolateral vertebral ossification of DISH together with a transverse fracture through the ankylosed thoracolumbar spine at T10–T12, i.e. a chalk-stick fracture. The disease-focused article title ('Thoracolumbar Pathological Fracture of Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis') and the in-text statement that the fracture occurred 'within the range of DISH' support DISH attribution despite the caption's mention of a metastatic lesion. B: Sagittal T1-weighted MRI demonstrates the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies with a fracture and altered marrow signal at T10–T12 in a spine with DISH. The DISH-focused article title and in-text statement that the fracture occurred within the range of DISH support attribution to DISH; the chalk-stick fracture is a recognized complication of the ankylosed DISH spine. panels.rationale: Single figure (no panel letters in image or caption) containing sagittal cervical-spine MRI views from a human patient. The caption explicitly states findings consistent with DISH with relatively preserved intervertebral disc heights, and clear spinal cord compression with marked reduction of the surrounding CSF space; the article title (DISH With Cervical Myelopathy) and prior caption triage (radiology, keep, real patient image, not third-party) confirm DISH attribution. The dominant additional finding is cord compression/CSF effacement (cervical myelopathy), which is not in the allowed vocabulary and is therefore listed under proposed_findings. DISH most characteristically involves the thoracic spine, so a cervical presentation with myelopathy is treated as a recognized less-common (variant) form. No skin is shown; no ethnicity is stated (the 'Sudan' origin in the title is not a stated patient ethnicity and is not inferred); age is not given for this figure. Modality remains MRI even though the image is a photograph of the displayed film; no diagnostic arrows/callipers are present (only scale/orientation text and blurred identifiers).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Left sagittal MRI is from the DISH case report and shows the T3-T4 anterior spondylolisthesis/cord-compression lesion; anterolateral DISH-type vertebral ossification is also visible on the sagittal image. B: Middle sagittal MRI shows the responsible T10/11 lesion described in the caption: anterior spondylolisthesis, severe cord compression, and T2 hyperintensity, in a disease-focused DISH case report. C: Axial MRI is the cross-sectional correlate of the captioned T10/11 severe cord compression in the same DISH case; the arrow marks the compressed canal/cord level.

in_text_mentions: mpression. Cervical and thoracic spine MRI revealed anterior spondylolisthesis and severe cord compression at T3 to T4 and T10 to T11, and high signal intensity on a T2-weighted image at T10/11 (Fig. 1). An X-ray revealed intervertebral disc space narrowing and anterior spondylolisthesis at T3/4 and T10/11 (Fig. 2). A myelogram-computed tomography (CT) scan showed anterior spondylolisthesis and severe cord compression at the T10/11 level. OPLL and OLF were not seen at T10/11. DISH was noted above the T10 level (Fig. 3). We determined that the lesion responsible was located at the T10/11 level.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real axial T2-weighted patient MRI through C3 in a case report whose title attributes dysphagia to DISH. The panel shows the pharyngeal cavity nearly closed (arrowhead) adjacent to the C3 vertebral body, i.e. extrinsic pharyngeal compression by the cervical spine, the recognized DISH manifestation (anterior cervical osteophyte-related hypopharyngeal narrowing). The red-arrow high T2 signal in the prevertebral space is, per the in-text, post-biopsy perforation/edema (a procedural complication), so it is not used to establish DISH attribution and no vocabulary key is assigned to it. Attribution rests on the captioned pharyngeal narrowing plus the disease-focused title; osteophytes themselves are not directly depicted on MRI, so confidence is moderate. B: Companion axial T2-weighted patient MRI through C4 in the same DISH case report. It shows the pharyngeal lumen nearly effaced (arrow) against the C4 vertebral body, consistent with extrinsic...

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Sagittal reconstructed CT of a human patient showing extensive flowing anterolateral ossification with thoracolumbar ankylosis consistent with DISH, together with spontaneous L4/L5 dislocation at the last mobile segment; attribution supported by the caption, in-text mention, and the disease-focused article title. B: Axial CT at L4/L5 of the same DISH patient showing disruption of the posterior elements with facet separation, i.e. a structural-failure complication of the ankylosed DISH spine; disease attribution is explicit in the caption, in-text mention, and article title.

panels.rationale: Single axial (transverse) CT through the cervical spine at the C3-C4 level in a real patient. A large anterior cervical osteophyte (orange arrow) projects into and narrows the upper airway, matching the caption and the disease-focused article title on cervical DISH. This is a specific, visible manifestation of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, so the panel is included. The esophageal-compression vocabulary key is not used because the caption specifies the upper airway, not the esophagus; airway compression is added as a proposed finding. No age, ethnicity, or skin assessment is applicable/stated.

panels.rationale: Single axial CT of the neck in a DISH case report; caption and in-text explicitly describe large cervical osteophytes at C2-C3 with a bony bridge between adjacent osteophytes causing airway impression, directly matching anterior cervical osteophytes and anterior longitudinal ligament bone bridging. Orange arrow annotation present. No ethnicity or age stated; no skin visible.

panels.figure_caption: Transverse computed tomography demonstrating a bony bridge between adjacent osteophytes, causing a left impression on the airway. The arrow pointing to the osteophytes at the C2-C3 vertebral level.
in_text_mentions: Following his admission, a computed tomography (CT) scan was performed. CT scan evaluation was invaluable in revealing the presence of large mass-occupying cervical osteophytes which resulted in the vocal cord paresis (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Single-image figure from a DISH-phagia case report. Endoscopic view of a real patient shows deformed and stenotic hypopharynx with no mucosal lesions, interpreted as extrinsic compression due to DISH. The panel directly illustrates the DISH-related manifestation dysphagia/hypopharyngeal stenosis.
panels.attribution_text: Soares et al. Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH)-Phagia: A Case Report and Review of Literature of a Rare Disease Manifestation.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.47221. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Flexible endoscopy revealing a deformed and stenotic hypopharynx.
in_text_mentions: nt was then submitted to a flexible endoscopy that revealed a deformed and stenotic hypopharynx with no mucosal lesions, suggesting extrinsic compression of the hypopharynx and high esophagus (Figure 2). The classical diagnostic criteria for DISH include three major elements: the presence of vertebral flowing ossifications present at a minimum of four contiguous vertebrae, preservation of disc height, and lack of significant degenerative changes at the involved vertebral segments, which differentiates DISH from degenerative spondylosis. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Gross specimen photograph of the atlas (C1) from a human patient with DISH (disease-focused article title: DISH of upper cervical vertebrae). Caption identifies an osteophyte of the anterior longitudinal ligament on the anterior arch (green arrow) and an alar ligament osteophyte (red arrow) — specific ligamentous ossification/enthesopathy manifestations of DISH. Real human bone specimen, readable, no third-party copyright indicated. b: Gross specimen photograph, posterior view of the same C1 specimen from a DISH patient. Caption demonstrates an osteophyte of the alar ligament (red arrow), an insertional enthesophyte at a spinal ligament attachment — a DISH manifestation in the craniocervical junction. Same human specimen as panel (a), no copyright issue. c: Gross specimen photograph, superior view of the same C1 specimen from a DISH patient. A red arrow is visible pointing to the superior aspect of the vertebra at the alar ligament...

panels.figure_caption: The atlas (C1 vertebra) viewed from different aspects. (a) shows the anterior view; osteophyte of the anterior longitudinal ligament in the anterior arch is identified (green arrow) along with osteophyte of the alar ligament (red arrow). (b) demonstrates the posterior view of osteophyte of the alar ligament (red arrow). (c) shows the superior view of the C1. (d) shows the inferior view.
in_text_mentions: In the atlas (C1) (Figure 1), osteophytes of the ALL (green arrow) and alar ligament (red arrow) are demonstrated in anterior and posterior views. In the upper cervical vertebrae (C1-C3) (Figure 2), similar changes are noted with clearer visualization of C1 osteophytes. The axis (C2) (Figure 3) shows a prominent osteophyte of the ALL (green arrow), while the C3 vertebra (Figure 4) also demonstrates an ALL osteophyte (green arrow).
